title: Franklin County 2026 Triennial Review: Last Day for Informal Sessions
author: CRE News Staff
excerpt: Today is the final day for Franklin County property owners to request an informal review of their tentative 2026 assessed values. Here is what the process covers, what comes next, and why the outcome matters for Columbus-area investors and landlords.

body:
Today, September 5, 2026, is the final day for Franklin County property owners to participate in an in-person or virtual informal review of their tentative 2026 assessed values — the simplest, no-cost way to contest the county's third triennial reappraisal since 2020. Owners who miss the informal window still have a formal path through the Franklin County Board of Revision, which opens after final values are published in December.

## What the 2026 Triennial Update Is

Ohio law requires county auditors to reappraise every property in their county every six years and to update assessed values every three years in between. Franklin County's 2026 update is a triennial — a mid-cycle recalibration based on recent sales data, not a full physical reappraisal. The last triennial was in 2023.

The Franklin County Auditor's Office sent notices of tentative 2026 appraised values to all property owners earlier this summer. Assessed value in Ohio is set at 35 percent of appraised value; that fraction is the number used to calculate the property tax bill. A property the Auditor values at $300,000 is assessed at $105,000, and the tax levy is applied to that assessed figure.

For context, Columbus-area home prices have risen roughly 6.2 percent year-over-year through mid-2026, [according to Redfin market data](https://www.redfin.com/city/4664/OH/Columbus/housing-market), with a median sale price around $304,000. Triennial updates in rising markets tend to push assessed values up, which translates directly to higher annual tax bills if the new value is not challenged.

## What the Informal Review Covers

An informal review is a meeting — held in person at locations across Franklin County or by video — between the property owner and Auditor's appraisal staff. Owners present evidence they believe supports a different value: recent comparable sales, a current appraisal, income-and-expense data for commercial or rental properties, or documented condition problems the Auditor's record does not reflect.

Staff can adjust a tentative value at the informal stage without the owner filing a legal complaint. That is the principal advantage of the informal review: it is faster, free, and does not require an attorney. For investors and landlords holding multiple Franklin County properties, even a modest reduction per parcel multiplied across a portfolio can translate to meaningful annual savings.

The informal review does not bind either party. If staff reduces a value at the informal stage, that reduction stands unless the county's own review process changes it. If staff confirms the value and the owner disagrees, the Board of Revision process remains available.

## Today's Deadline and What Remains Open

In-person and virtual informal review sessions run through today, September 5. The Franklin County Auditor's Office has been scheduling sessions since July; [NBC4 reported the Auditor launched a dedicated website for the update](https://www.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/franklin-county/franklin-county-auditor-launches-website-for-property-value-update/) to guide owners through the informal process.

Some sources covering the 2026 informal process have noted that property owners who cannot attend a session may be able to submit supporting documents online after September 5; the Auditor's website at [auditor.franklincountyohio.gov](https://auditor.franklincountyohio.gov) is the authoritative reference for whether a document-only submission path remains open and through what date. CREN was unable to confirm a specific document-only deadline through a direct Auditor source as of this writing.

## After September: What Happens to Values and When

After the informal review window closes, the Auditor's Office submits updated tentative values to the Ohio Department of Taxation for review. The Department checks values for statistical uniformity across the county — a step designed to catch systemic over- or under-assessment. Final appraised values are expected to be issued in December 2026, [according to reporting on the process](https://www.nbc4i.com/news/local-news/franklin-county/franklin-county-auditor-launches-website-for-property-value-update/).

Owners have time between the final value notice and the Board of Revision filing window to evaluate whether a formal challenge makes sense. Attorneys who handle property tax appeals routinely recommend that owners review final values in December and seek comparable sales data before filing.

## The Board of Revision: The Formal Appeal Path

Property owners who did not participate in the informal review, or who remain dissatisfied after an informal decision, can file a formal complaint with the [Franklin County Board of Revision](https://auditor.franklincountyohio.gov/Real-Estate). The Board of Revision — a three-member body composed of the County Auditor, County Treasurer, and County Commissioners — holds hearings and has authority to increase, decrease, or confirm a property's value.

In Ohio, the standard BOR filing deadline is April 1 of the tax year following the valuation — meaning complaints contesting 2026 values would be filed by April 1, 2027. Filing requires a formal complaint form and supporting evidence; legal representation is not mandatory but is common for commercial property owners given the complexity of income-approach arguments.

A BOR decision can be appealed to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or to the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas. Those pathways exist for both owners who believe the BOR reduced a value too little and for school districts or other taxing entities that believe a value was reduced too much.

## Why This Matters for Investment Properties

For owners of rental properties, the triennial update feeds directly into operating costs. Ohio's property tax system does not have a separate commercial rate; assessed value drives the bill regardless of use. A fourplex, a mixed-use building on a neighborhood commercial corridor, or an industrial warehouse — all assessed on the same framework.

Owners of income-producing property making the case at an informal review or BOR hearing can present income-and-expense data, including rent rolls and vacancy rates, as evidence of what the market will bear. An assessment based on comparable sales of owner-occupied residences may not accurately reflect the economics of a rental property in the same location, which is a recognized argument under Ohio property tax law.

The Franklin County Auditor's Office does not release property-specific informal review outcomes. Investors interested in whether particular corridors or property classes saw systematic assessment increases can track parcel-level data through the Auditor's online property search at [auditor.franklincountyohio.gov](https://auditor.franklincountyohio.gov).

## What to Watch

The next concrete checkpoint is December 2026, when the Ohio Department of Taxation is expected to certify final appraised values for Franklin County. At that point, owners will have the information they need to decide whether to file a Board of Revision complaint before the April 1, 2027 deadline. The BOR's case load and hearing schedule for 2027 — and whether it mirrors the volume seen after the 2023 triennial — will be a secondary indicator of how widely owners contested the update.
